title: Our Sun: why its light warms things, and why we never look at it

summary.text: Sunlight feels gentle on your skin, yet a magnifying glass can gather it into a dot that makes paper smoke. The Sun is a star, a huge ball of very hot gas, and the nearest star to us. About 109 Earths would fit across its face. It shines because deep inside it, hydrogen is squeezed into helium, which gives out energy. It is not a fire. Its light crosses space in about 8 minutes, and turns into heat wherever something absorbs it, such as black paper, a road or your skin. The lens inside your eye gathers light just as a magnifying glass does, so looking straight at the Sun can harm your eyes for ever. We watch the Sun safely through its reflections, shadows and pictures on a wall.
summary.art: A child on a sunny balcony holding a steel plate with a sheet of black paper, while her mother holds a magnifying glass above it and a thin thread of smoke rises from a tiny bright dot. In the sky above, the Sun is drawn as a glowing ball, with a small Earth beside it for size.

intro.hook: Stand in a patch of sunlight from a window for one minute. Then step into the shade next to it. Which feels warmer? That sunlight has just crossed 150 million kilometres of nearly empty space, where there is almost nothing to warm. So where does the warmth on your skin come from?
intro.text: The warmth is made right on your skin. Sunlight is a kind of energy, and when your skin absorbs it, the light turns into heat. In this unit you gather sunlight with a magnifying glass and find out how much heat is hiding in it. You also find out what the Sun is, how it makes its light without any fire, and why the lens in your own eye means you must never look straight at it.
intro.art: A girl standing half in a bright patch of sunlight on a tiled floor by a window and half in the shade, holding out both hands, one lit and one in shadow.

outcomes: I can explain that the Sun is a star, a huge ball of very hot gas, and the nearest star to the Earth.
I can explain that the Sun makes its light by joining hydrogen into helium in its core, and that it is not a fire.
I can explain that sunlight turns into heat where something absorbs it, and that black things absorb more sunlight than white things.
I can help run a fair test with a magnifying glass, with a grown-up, and show that gathered sunlight is far hotter than spread-out sunlight.
I can explain why looking straight at the Sun harms the eyes, and name safe ways to watch the Sun.
I can say how living things use sunlight: plants make food with it, and animals such as lizards warm up in it.
I can tell how people found out that the Sun is not a giant fire.

terms.meaning: A huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is a star.
terms.example: The stars you see at night are suns too. They look tiny because they are very far away.
terms.art: The Sun drawn large on one side of the page, and a sprinkle of tiny stars in a dark sky on the other side.

terms.meaning: The star at the centre of our solar system. The Earth and the other planets go round it.
terms.example: The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from the Earth. Its light takes about 8 minutes to reach us.
terms.art: The Sun as a glowing ball, with a tiny Earth far away on a dotted path round it.

terms.meaning: What makes things happen: move, warm up, light up or grow. Sunlight carries energy.
terms.example: Sunlight dries the clothes on the line and warms the balcony floor. Both need energy.
terms.art: Clothes drying on a balcony line in bright sunshine, with small wavy lines rising from a wet towel.

terms.meaning: To take in. When a thing absorbs light, the light goes into it and turns into heat.
terms.example: A black umbrella gets hot in the sun, because it absorbs most of the light that falls on it.
terms.art: Arrows of sunlight going into a black umbrella and stopping there, with small heat lines rising.

terms.meaning: To send light back. A shiny or white surface reflects most of the light that falls on it.
terms.example: A white wall stays cooler than a dark one in the sun, because it reflects most of the light.
terms.art: Arrows of sunlight bouncing off a white wall.

terms.meaning: Energy that makes things warmer. Heat moves from warmer things to cooler things.
terms.example: The heat from a sunny tile floor goes into your feet, so the tiles feel warm.
terms.art: Bare feet on sunny floor tiles, with small heat arrows going up into the feet.

terms.meaning: A clear, curved piece of glass or plastic that bends light. A lens that is thicker in the middle can gather light to a point.
terms.example: A magnifying glass is a lens. So are the glasses some people wear, and there is one inside each of your eyes.
terms.art: A magnifying glass seen from the side, with lines of sunlight bending through it and meeting at a point below.

terms.meaning: To gather light into one small spot. The spot where the light meets is also called the focus.
terms.example: Lift a magnifying glass slowly above paper in the sun. The bright circle shrinks to a tiny dot. That dot is the focus.
terms.art: Three pictures side by side: a big bright circle under a lens held low, a smaller circle, and a tiny dot when the lens is higher.

terms.meaning: The very centre of the Sun, where its energy is made. It is about 15 million degrees Celsius.
terms.example: Almost all the Sun's energy is made in its core, the inner quarter of the way out from the centre.
terms.art: The Sun cut in half like an orange, with a small, white-hot ball at the centre labelled core.

terms.meaning: The two lightest kinds of atom. The Sun is made mostly of hydrogen, with most of the rest helium.
terms.example: Helium is the gas that makes balloons float. Most of the Sun's helium was made from hydrogen.
terms.art: A balloon seller with helium balloons, and beside them a big Sun with the letters H and He on it.

terms.meaning: Joining the centres of tiny atoms together. In the Sun's core, hydrogen joins to make helium, and this gives out energy.
terms.example: Fusion makes all the Sun's light. It does not need air, so the Sun is not burning like a fire.
terms.art: Four small dots labelled hydrogen coming together into one bigger dot labelled helium, with a flash of light.

terms.meaning: A thin layer at the back of the eye that catches light and sends signals to the brain.
terms.example: The lens in your eye focuses light onto your retina. That makes a picture you can see.
terms.art: A simple cut-away drawing of an eye, light entering at the front and meeting at the back on a pink layer labelled retina.

terms.meaning: Light from the Sun that our eyes cannot see. It can burn skin and fade colours.
terms.example: A curtain that hangs in a sunny window fades, mostly because of ultraviolet light.
terms.art: A curtain by a window, faded pale at the edge where sunlight falls, and bright where it is folded.

terms.meaning: Light from the Sun that our eyes cannot see, but our skin feels as warmth.
terms.example: About half of the Sun's energy reaching the ground comes as infrared light.
terms.art: A child with eyes closed, face turned away from the Sun, feeling warmth on her cheek, with faint red lines drawn in the air.

terms.meaning: How plants make their food from sunlight, water and air.
terms.example: A tulsi plant on the windowsill photosynthesises with the sunlight that reaches her leaves.
terms.art: A tulsi plant in a pot on a sunny windowsill, with arrows of sunlight landing on her leaves.

terms.meaning: To lie in the sunshine to get warm.
terms.example: A garden lizard basks on a sunny wall in the morning, to warm her body before she hunts.
terms.art: A garden lizard spread flat on a sunny wall in the morning.

terms.meaning: When the Moon passes between the Sun and the Earth and hides part or all of the Sun.
terms.example: During an eclipse, many people are tempted to look at the Sun. It is just as harmful then as on any other day.
terms.art: A dark Moon covering half of the Sun, drawn as a picture on a wall made by a mirror.

terms.meaning: Special glasses with a dark filter that lets through only a tiny part of the Sun's light. Safe ones are marked ISO 12312-2.
terms.example: Ordinary sunglasses let through far too much light to look at the Sun. Only eclipse glasses made for this are safe.
terms.art: A pair of cardboard eclipse glasses with very dark lenses next to ordinary sunglasses with a red cross.

terms.meaning: A flat panel that turns sunlight straight into electricity.
terms.example: Many buildings in India now have solar panels on the roof, and some have solar water heaters too.
terms.art: Blue solar panels on the flat roof of an apartment building in sunshine.

explanations.definition: A star is a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. The Sun is a star, and the nearest one to the Earth.
explanations.description: The Sun looks much bigger and brighter than the stars at night only because it is so much closer. It is about 150 million kilometres away. The next nearest star is about 270,000 times further. The Sun is about 109 times as wide as the Earth, and more than a million Earths would fit inside it. It holds almost all the material in the solar system: more than 99 parts in every 100. Most of the Sun is hydrogen, the lightest kind of atom, and most of the rest is helium. Its glowing surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius. That is hot enough to melt any rock or metal.
examples: If the Earth were a small marble, 1 centimetre wide, the Sun would be a ball more than a metre wide.
The Sun is not the biggest star. Many stars are much bigger, and many are much smaller.
explanations.art: A tiny Earth next to a curved edge of the Sun that fills most of the page, to show the size.
explanations.context: This card says what the Sun is, how big it is, and what it is made of.

explanations.concept: How the Sun makes its light
explanations.definition: In the Sun's core, the centres of hydrogen atoms are squeezed together so hard that they join to make helium. This is called nuclear fusion, and it gives out the energy that becomes sunlight.
explanations.description: Many people think the Sun is on fire. It is not. A fire needs oxygen from the air, and there is no air in space. The Sun's core is about 15 million degrees Celsius, and the weight of the whole Sun presses down on it. There, hydrogen is joined into helium. A helium atom made this way weighs a tiny bit less than the four hydrogen atoms that made it. The missing bit of material turns into energy. Every second, the Sun turns about 4 million tonnes of its material into energy. The Sun is so big that it has shone like this for about 4.6 billion years, and will go on for about 5 billion more.
examples: A fire the size of the Sun, burning coal, would have burnt out in a few thousand years. The Sun is about a million times older than that.
Fusion needs no air. That is why the Sun shines in empty space.
explanations.art: Four small hydrogen dots squeezing together into one helium dot in the Sun's core, with a burst of light spreading outwards.
explanations.context: This card answers a common question: is the Sun burning? Here is what really makes its light.

explanations.concept: How long sunlight takes to reach us
explanations.description: Once light leaves the Sun's surface, it reaches the Earth in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds. Scientists measure that very exactly. Inside the Sun, the energy's trip is much slower. The Sun's insides are so packed that the energy is taken in and given out again countless times, in random directions, on its way from the core to the surface. Scientists work out how long this takes from models of the inside of the Sun, because nobody can see in there. Their answers range from about 10,000 years to about 170,000 years. So the sunlight on your skin today began its journey in the core many thousands of years ago, and spent only its last 8 minutes crossing space.
examples: The sunshine on your balcony at lunchtime left the Sun's surface at about a quarter to one, 8 minutes earlier.
If the Sun stopped shining, we would not know for about 8 minutes.

perspectives.who: Scientists who use one kind of Sun model
perspectives.explanation: The energy takes about 170,000 years to work its way out. NASA often gives this number.
It could be as short as about 10,000 years. The answer depends on how packed the Sun's insides are, which can only be worked out, not seen.

explanations.art: A wiggly zigzag line inside the Sun from the core to the surface, then one straight arrow across space to a small Earth, labelled 8 minutes.
explanations.context: This card is about the journey of sunlight. Part of it is measured exactly, and part can only be worked out.

explanations.concept: Sunlight turns into heat where it is absorbed
explanations.definition: Sunlight is energy. When a thing absorbs sunlight, that energy makes its tiny particles jiggle faster, and we feel that as heat.
explanations.description: Space between the Sun and the Earth is nearly empty, so there is almost nothing there to absorb the light and warm up. The warmth appears only when the light lands on something. A black thing absorbs most of the light that falls on it, so it gets hot quickly. A white thing reflects most of the light, so it stays cooler. Even the air is warmed mostly from below. Sunlight passes through clear air, warms the ground, and the warm ground then warms the air above it. That is why a black road in Chennai in May can be far too hot to stand on barefoot, while a white wall nearby is only warm.
examples: A black car parked in the sun gets hotter inside than a white car parked beside it.
Roofs painted white keep the rooms under them cooler, because the white paint reflects most of the sunlight.
explanations.art: Sunlight falling on a black road and a white wall side by side: the arrows go into the road with heat lines rising, and bounce off the wall.
explanations.context: This card answers the puzzle from the start of the unit: where does the warmth of sunlight come from?

explanations.concept: A lens gathers sunlight into a dot
explanations.definition: A magnifying glass is a lens that is thicker in the middle. It bends the sunlight passing through it, so that all the light meets in one small spot, the focus.
explanations.description: Hold a magnifying glass just above paper in the sun, and you see a bright circle about as big as the lens. Lift it slowly, and the circle shrinks to a tiny, dazzling dot. The lens has made no new light. It has only taken all the light that falls on the glass and packed it into a much smaller place. A magnifying glass about 5 centimetres wide can pack the light from its whole face into a dot smaller than a grain of rice. So the dot gets hundreds of times more light than the same patch of paper in plain sunshine. Black paper absorbs that light and gets hot enough to smoke within seconds. The dot is really a tiny picture of the Sun, which is why it is round.
examples: A glass bottle of water left on a sunny windowsill can act as a lens. Fires have been started this way.
A magnifying glass must never be left lying in sunlight, near curtains or papers.
explanations.art: A magnifying glass above black paper, with lines of sunlight bending through it and meeting in a tiny bright dot, and a thin thread of smoke.
explanations.context: This card explains what happened in the Sun Dot experiment, when a magnifying glass made paper smoke.

explanations.concept: Why we never look straight at the Sun
explanations.definition: The eye has its own lens. If you look at the Sun, that lens focuses the Sun's light into a tiny bright spot on the retina, at the back of the eye, and this harms the retina's cells.
explanations.description: The eye's lens works much like a magnifying glass. It focuses light from the things you look at into a small picture on your retina. That is how you see. When you look at the Sun, the picture of the Sun on your retina is a tiny, fierce dot of light. The retina has no pain nerves, so you feel nothing while it is being harmed. The harm can show only hours later, as a blurred or dark spot in the middle of what you see. It can last for ever. Sunglasses do not make it safe. They let through far too much light. Binoculars and telescopes are even worse, because they gather more light. During a solar eclipse the Sun is just as harmful, and people are more tempted to stare. Safe ways to watch the Sun are its picture on a wall, made by a pinhole or a mirror, or eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2.
examples: After solar eclipses, eye doctors in many countries, India among them, have treated people whose eyes were harmed by looking at the Sun.
Never look at the Sun through a magnifying glass, binoculars, a camera viewfinder or a telescope.
explanations.art: A cut-away eye with the Sun's light entering and meeting in one tiny dot on the retina at the back, next to a magnifying glass making a dot on paper.
explanations.context: This card explains the rule that matters most in this unit: never look straight at the Sun, and why.

explanations.concept: The light we cannot see: infrared and ultraviolet
explanations.definition: Sunlight carries more than the light we see. Infrared light is beyond red, and we feel it as warmth. Ultraviolet light is beyond violet, and it can burn skin and fade colours.
explanations.description: In 1800, William Herschel, an astronomer in England, split sunlight into a rainbow with a prism. He put thermometers in each colour, and one just past the red end, where he could see no light at all. That last thermometer got the warmest. He had found infrared light. A year later, Johann Ritter in Germany found ultraviolet light beyond the violet end, because it darkened a chemical that light darkens. About half of the Sun's energy that reaches the ground is infrared. A small part is ultraviolet. Ultraviolet light is what tans and burns skin, yellows old newspaper and fades a curtain in a sunny window. Our skin also uses a little of it to make vitamin D, which keeps bones strong.
examples: A shirt left on the line for weeks fades on the side that faces the Sun.
You can feel the warmth of sunlight on your closed eyelids, even though infrared light is invisible.
explanations.art: A rainbow of light from a prism on a table, with thermometers in each colour and one past the red end reading the highest.
explanations.context: This card is about the parts of sunlight that our eyes cannot see, and what they do.

explanations.definition: Almost all life on Earth runs on sunlight. Plants catch it to make food, and animals use its warmth.
explanations.description: A plant cannot walk to find food. She makes her own. Her leaves catch sunlight and use its energy to make sugar from water and air. This is photosynthesis. A plant on a dark shelf grows long and pale as she reaches for light, and a plant by a window turns her leaves towards the light. Animals that eat plants, and animals that eat those animals, are all living on that caught sunlight. A garden lizard has a different problem. Her body does not make much heat of its own, so on a cool morning she is slow and cannot chase insects. So she basks on a sunny wall, flat and wide, to absorb as much sunlight as she can. Once she is warm, she can move fast and hunt.
examples: The rice in your plate grew with sunlight that fell on a paddy field.
In the cool early morning, you can sometimes see a garden lizard or a skink lying still on a sunny wall.
explanations.art: A garden lizard flat on a sunlit compound wall, and below it a row of paddy plants with sunlight arrows landing on their leaves.
explanations.context: This card is about how plants and animals use the Sun's light and warmth.

explanations.definition: The Sun's light is a mix of all colours, and it is white. It looks yellow or orange from the ground because the air scatters some of its blue light away.
explanations.description: Children often draw the Sun yellow. Seen from space, the Sun is white. Our air scatters blue light more than the other colours. That scattered blue light is what makes the sky blue. With some blue taken out, the Sun looks a little yellow from the ground. At sunrise and sunset, the light passes through much more air, so even more blue and green are scattered away, and the Sun looks orange or red. You can check the Sun's real colour safely: its picture on a white wall, made by a mirror at midday, looks white.
examples: Photos of the Sun taken by astronauts in space show it white.
At sunset over the sea at Kanyakumari, the Sun looks deep orange.
explanations.art: Three suns in a row: white in a black sky from space, pale yellow at noon in a blue sky, and orange at sunset over the sea.
explanations.context: This card answers a question children often ask: is the Sun really yellow?

agreed.text: The Sun is a star, the nearest one to the Earth, and it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
agreed.evidence: The colours in sunlight show which atoms are in the Sun. Other stars show the same kinds of colours.

agreed.text: The Sun shines by nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen into helium in its core.
agreed.evidence: Fusion gives out tiny particles called neutrinos. Huge detectors deep underground, in Japan, Canada and elsewhere, catch neutrinos from the Sun's core, in about the numbers fusion predicts.

agreed.text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth.
agreed.evidence: We know the speed of light and the distance to the Sun very exactly. The distance is measured by bouncing radar signals off the planets.

agreed.text: Looking straight at the Sun can harm the retina for ever, and ordinary sunglasses do not protect it.
agreed.evidence: Eye doctors around the world, including in India, find damage to the centre of the retina in people who watched an eclipse without safe filters.

agreed.text: Sunlight turns into heat where it is absorbed, and dark things absorb more of it than light-coloured things.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with black and white paper in the sun. Thermometers and heat cameras show the same.

challenging.claim: The Sun is a giant fire.
challenging.who: A very common idea, and what many scientists thought until the 1800s
challenging.for: The Sun is hot and bright, like a fire, and it gives out heat and light.
challenging.against: A fire needs oxygen, and space has none. A fire as big as the Sun would have burnt out in a few thousand years, but the Earth's rocks show the Sun has shone for billions of years. The Sun shines by fusion.
challenging.context: Is the Sun burning? This card looks at a very common idea.

challenging.claim: Sunglasses make it safe to look at the Sun.
challenging.for: Sunglasses make the Sun look much less bright, so it feels comfortable.
challenging.against: Even dark sunglasses let through thousands of times too much of the Sun's light, and some harmful light we cannot see. The retina has no pain nerves, so it gives no warning. Only eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2 are safe for looking at the Sun.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake that can harm eyes for ever.

challenging.who: Most children's drawings, and many grown-ups
challenging.for: From the ground, the Sun often looks pale yellow, and orange at sunrise and sunset.
challenging.against: From space, astronauts see a white Sun. The air scatters some blue light away, which makes the Sun look yellow from below.
challenging.context: What colour is the Sun really? This card looks at a common answer.

challenging.claim: The Sun is only harmful to look at during an eclipse.
challenging.who: A common idea, because warnings are given mostly before eclipses
challenging.for: Most cases of eye harm from the Sun happen just after eclipses.
challenging.against: The Sun is just as harmful on every day. During an eclipse, the sky gets darker, the eyes open wider, and people stare for longer. That is why more people are harmed then.
challenging.context: Why do warnings about the Sun come mostly before eclipses? This card explains.

challenging.claim: The Sun will go on shining for ever.
challenging.for: The Sun has shone every day of human history, and it looks the same each day.
challenging.against: The Sun is slowly using up the hydrogen in its core. In about 5 billion years it will swell into a huge red star, and later shrink into a small, fading white one.
challenging.context: Will the Sun last for ever? This card looks at what scientists expect.

big_questions.q: Sunlight felt gentle on your hand, yet the same light made paper smoke when a lens gathered it. Is sunlight gentle or fierce?
big_questions.hint: Think about the big circle and the tiny dot in your experiment. Was the light different, or only how much of it landed in one place?

big_questions.q: The light warming you now began its journey in the Sun's core many thousands of years ago. Is it old light or new light?
big_questions.hint: It spent thousands of years inside the Sun and only 8 minutes crossing space.

big_questions.q: Your eye's lens focuses sunlight onto a spot with no pain nerves. Why might a body not feel every kind of harm?
big_questions.hint: Think about which parts of your body hurt easily, like your fingers, and which do not, like your hair.

big_questions.q: Plants catch sunlight, animals eat plants, and you eat both. How much of you was once sunlight?
big_questions.hint: Follow your breakfast back, step by step, until you reach a plant in the sun.

big_questions.q: People in many lands, from the Konark temple in Odisha to old Egypt, honoured the Sun. Why do you think so many people, far apart, did the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about what would happen to the fields, the rain and the warmth without the Sun.

big_questions.q: The Earth catches only about one part in two billion of the Sun's light. The rest goes off into space. Is that a waste?
big_questions.hint: Some of that light reaches other planets, and some may reach someone far away, as starlight.

story.title: The Smoke on the Vadam Cloth
story.note: Made up. Nila, Arun, their Paati and their building in Chennai are invented. The science is real: a magnifying glass left in sunlight can scorch cloth, the eye's lens focuses sunlight onto the retina, and a covered mirror makes a safe picture of the Sun on a wall.
text: It was April in Chennai, and the sun on the terrace was so strong that the floor tiles were hot by nine in the morning. Nila was nine. Her little brother Arun was six. Every summer, their Paati made rice vadams, and every summer, the children helped to dry them.

Paati spread an old white veshti across the terrace floor and weighed down its corners with bricks. Nila pressed the soft rice dough through the brass mould, and little curly vadams dropped onto the cloth in rows. Arun was meant to help. Instead he lay on his back, squinting at the sky.
'Paati, does the Sun have spots?' he asked. 'My book says it has dark spots.'

'So I have heard,' said Paati. She took out her reading glass, the round magnifying glass she used for the small print in the newspaper. She read out the price of tomatoes, frowned, and put the glass down on the edge of the cloth. Then she went downstairs to bring more dough. Arun ran down after her.

Nila carried on pressing vadams. After a few minutes, she sniffed. Something smelt like a candle that had just been blown out. She looked around. At the edge of the cloth, where Paati's glass lay tilted on a brick, a thin grey thread of smoke was rising.

Nila jumped up and lifted the glass away. Under it, on the white cloth, was a brown spot as small as a mustard seed, with a black rim. It was still smoking. She poured water from her tumbler over it, and the smoke stopped.
When Paati came back, Nila showed her the spot. 'Your glass did this,' she said.
'My glass?' said Paati. 'It only makes the letters big.'
Nila thought about it. 'The glass is thick in the middle,' she said slowly. 'It bends the sunlight. Maybe it gathers all the light that falls on it into one little spot.'

'Show me,' said Paati. She tore a strip off the newspaper and put it on a steel plate. She held the glass above it herself, because she did not want Nila holding a lens in that sun. When she held it low, a big, soft circle of light lay on the paper. Nothing happened. When she lifted it slowly, the circle shrank. It became a tiny dot, so bright that Nila had to look away. Under the dot, a black letter began to smoke. It took only a few seconds. The white paper between the letters took much longer.
'The sun on my hand feels warm, not hot,' said Nila. 'But when the glass squeezes it into a dot, it burns.'

Just then Arun came up the stairs. He was wearing Amma's big sunglasses, and he had Appa's binoculars round his neck. 'I am going to look at the spots on the Sun,' he said. 'The sunglasses will make it safe.'
'Stop!' said Nila, and she stood in front of him.

She made him sit down by the brown spot on the cloth. 'Look at this,' she said. 'Paati's glass gathered the sunlight into a dot, and the dot burned the cloth. Your eye has a lens inside it too. It gathers light the same way, onto the back of your eye. If you look at the Sun, it makes a dot like this, right inside you. Binoculars are two big lenses. They would gather even more.'
'But I would feel it,' said Arun. 'I would shut my eyes.'

'That's the trouble,' said Paati quietly. 'The back of the eye has no pain nerves, so it gives no warning. When I was a girl, my cousin Ravi watched an eclipse with his bare eyes. It did not hurt at all. The next morning there was a grey patch in the middle of everything he looked at. It is still there, sixty years later.'
Arun took off the sunglasses. 'Then I can never see the Sun's spots,' he said, and his lip wobbled.
Nila thought again. 'We can see the Sun without looking at it,' she said. 'Paati, can I borrow your little mirror?'

Paati's small round mirror lived in her handbag. Nila covered it with a piece of paper and cut a square hole in the paper, about as wide as her fingernail. In the corner of the terrace was the door to the dark staircase. Its far wall was painted white. Nila stood in the sun and tilted the mirror until a patch of reflected light landed deep inside, on that white wall.
Arun ran in to look. On the wall was a round, white circle of light, about the size of a biscuit.
'It's round,' said Arun. 'But the hole is square.'
'Because it isn't a picture of the hole,' said Nila. 'It's a picture of the Sun.'

Arun stared at it for a long time. He could stare as long as he liked, because he was looking at a wall. He did not see any spots. 'They're too small for our little mirror,' said Nila. 'But this is the real Sun, and you can look at it as long as you want.'

By evening, the vadams were dry and crisp. Paati folded the veshti with the little brown spot in it. 'All day the sun dried my vadams, and nobody gathered it into any dot,' she said. 'And it nearly burned my veshti when one glass did.'
That night, Paati's reading glass went into her drawer, out of the sun. Arun gave Amma back her sunglasses, and asked Nila to make the wall Sun again the next day.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the magnifying glass made no new light. It gathered the sunlight falling on its whole face into one tiny dot, so that dot got hundreds of times more light than plain sunshine, and the cloth absorbed it as heat. The black letters smoked first because black absorbs more light than white. The eye's lens does the same job, focusing light onto the retina, which has no pain nerves. That is why looking at the Sun gives no warning, and why sunglasses and binoculars make it no safer. The covered mirror sent a beam of sunlight onto a dark wall. Far enough away, any small hole gives a round spot, because the spot is a picture of the round Sun.
ask: What did Paati's reading glass do to the sunlight, to make a spot on the cloth?
Why did the black letters on the newspaper smoke before the white paper?
Why did Nila say the sunglasses and binoculars would not make it safe for Arun?
Why was the spot of light on the wall round, when the hole in the paper was square?
Paati had used her glass for years without knowing it could burn. Nila worked it out in a few minutes. What did Nila do that helped her find the answer?

games.title: Safe or Not Safe? Ways to watch the Sun
games.context: This is a sorting card game. Each card shows a way people try to watch the Sun. Players decide whether it is safe or harmful, and say why.

Welder's glass, shade number 14 (SAFE)
Ordinary sunglasses (NOT SAFE)
Two or three pairs of sunglasses worn together (NOT SAFE)

Looking through a telescope with no special Sun filter (NOT SAFE)
Looking at the Sun for just one second (NOT SAFE)
Looking through an old X-ray film (NOT SAFE)
Looking through a piece of glass blackened with candle smoke (NOT SAFE)
Looking through a magnifying glass at the Sun (NOT SAFE)
Eclipse glasses with a scratch or a hole (NOT SAFE)
Looking at the Sun when it is half covered in an eclipse (NOT SAFE)
Looking at the Sun through a camera's eyepiece (NOT SAFE)
Looking at the Sun through a CD (NOT SAFE)

NOT SAFE: a picture of an eye with a red cross

items: Player name
Cards sorted right
Reasons given

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them face down.
On your turn, take the top card, read it out, and put it on SAFE or NOT SAFE.
Say why. A reason earns an extra point. A good reason uses the words lens, retina or picture.
Check the answer in the brackets. A right sort scores 1 point.
Playing alone? Sort all 20, then check them all and count your points.
The player with the most points wins.

flow.do: Lay out the sorting mat and shuffle the cards.
flow.say: Each card shows a way people try to watch the Sun. Some are safe, and some can harm your eyes for ever. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Each card is a way to watch the Sun. Is it safe or not safe? Sort them!
flow.context: This is the first step of Safe or Not Safe, a sorting game about ways to watch the Sun.

flow.do: Play the card 'Ordinary sunglasses' as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Ordinary sunglasses. Safe or not safe?
flow.kid: Practice card. Ordinary sunglasses. Safe or not safe?

check.q: Is it safe to look at the Sun through ordinary sunglasses?
options: Yes, because they make the Sun look dim
No, they still let through far too much light
check.why: Sunglasses make the Sun look dimmer, so it feels comfortable. But they still let through thousands of times too much light. The lens in your eye focuses it onto the retina, which has no pain nerves to warn you. Picking 'yes' is what many grown-ups think too, and it is a dangerous mistake.

flow.do: Take turns to sort the rest of the cards, giving a reason each time.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card, sort it, and tell us why.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Sort it. Say why!
flow.parent: Listen for reasons that mention the eye's lens focusing the Sun's light onto the retina. The safe ways all have one thing in common: you look at a picture of the Sun, or through a filter made for it, never at the Sun itself.

flow.do: Count the points and talk about the pattern.
flow.say: Look at the SAFE column. What do most of these have in common?
flow.kid: Look at all the safe cards. What do they have in common?

check.q: What do the colander, the pinhole viewer and the mirror picture have in common?
options: You look at a picture of the Sun, not at the Sun
They all make the Sun look bigger
They are all dark glass
check.why: In all three, sunlight makes a picture on a wall or on paper, and you look at the picture with your back to the Sun. Picking 'they make the Sun look bigger' is not right: the pictures are usually small. What makes them safe is that no lens gathers the Sun's light into your eye.

rules: Every sunbeam starts on square 0, the Sun's core.
On your turn, another player reads you a card. Answer right, roll the dice and move. Answer wrong, move 1 square.
On a TRY IT card, do it. Then roll and move.
Follow what the square says: BUMP, FAST LANE, MAGNIFYING GLASS or CLOUD.
When you reach the Earth, choose where to land and say what happens to you there. On a leaf, you become food. On a black road, you become heat. On a white wall, you are reflected.

flow.do: Set up the board. Put every sunbeam on square 0.
flow.say: You are each a bit of the Sun's energy, just made in the core. The inside of the Sun is crowded, so you will get bumped back. Space is empty, so you will speed along.
flow.kid: You are a sunbeam in the Sun's core. Get out of the Sun and race to the Earth!
flow.context: This is the first step of Sunbeam Race, a board game about the journey of sunlight from the Sun's core to the Earth.

flow.do: Play the game, taking turns.
flow.say: Read the card, answer, and roll. Watch out for the bump squares inside the Sun.
flow.kid: Answer the card. Roll the dice. Move your sunbeam. Watch out for bumps!

check.q: Why does the board have bump squares inside the Sun, but a fast lane in space?
options: Inside the Sun, energy keeps getting taken in and sent out again. Space is nearly empty.
Space has more air
The Sun's core is cold
check.why: Inside the Sun, energy is taken in and given out again countless times, in random directions, so it takes thousands of years to get out. In space there is almost nothing in the way, so light crosses to the Earth in about 8 minutes. Picking 'space has more air' is the wrong way round: space has almost no air at all.

flow.do: When a player lands, they say what happens to their sunbeam.
flow.say: Where did you land? What happens to you now?
flow.kid: Where did you land? Say what happens to you now.
flow.parent: A good answer: on the black road, I am absorbed and turn into heat, so the road gets hot. On the leaf, the plant uses me to make her food. On the white wall, most of me is reflected.

experiments.title: The Sun Dot: when does sunlight make paper smoke?
experiments.question: Sunlight only warms paper. Does it make paper smoke when a magnifying glass gathers it into a tiny dot? And does black paper or white paper smoke first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When the magnifying glass makes a big circle of sunlight on black paper, what will happen? When it makes a tiny dot, what will happen? Will black paper or white paper smoke first, or neither? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same magnifying glass, the same steel plate and the same sunshine for every try. In part 1, only the size of the spot changes: a big circle, then a tiny dot. In part 2, only the colour of the paper changes. Try each paper 3 times, on a fresh spot each time, because one try can be a fluke. Stop counting at 60 seconds.

materials.item: a magnifying glass at least 5 cm across. Reading glasses for long sight may work, but more slowly.
a sheet of black chart paper, or a sheet of paper coloured all over with a black crayon or marker
a sheet of plain white paper
a steel plate or a steel thali, to put the paper on
a tumbler of water, to put out any smouldering paper
a clock with a seconds hand, or a phone timer
a sunny balcony, terrace or open window, between about 10 in the morning and 3 in the afternoon
sunglasses for the grown-up and child to wear while watching the dot on the paper (they protect from the glare of the dot, not for looking at the Sun)

experiments.safety: A grown-up holds the magnifying glass the whole time. Never look at the Sun, and never look at the Sun through the lens. Never point the dot at skin, at anyone, or at clothes, curtains or plants. Work on a steel plate, away from anything that can burn. Stop as soon as you see smoke and move the lens away. Pour water on the paper at the end. Put the lens away indoors in a drawer, because a lens left in the sun can start a fire.

schedule.what: On a sunny day, make a big circle and a tiny dot of sunlight on black paper. Then compare black and white paper. Count the seconds until smoke.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the lens, the paper and the light: once for the big circle and once for the tiny dot.

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot in direct sunshine, on a balcony, a terrace or at an open window. 2. Put the steel plate on the floor there, away from curtains and plants. 3. Put the black paper on the plate, and the tumbler of water beside it. 4. Put on sunglasses, both of you.
flow.say: Today we gather sunlight with a magnifying glass. I will hold the glass, and you will watch and count. There is one rule above all. We never look at the Sun, not even through the glass.
flow.kid: Find a sunny spot. Put the steel plate down. Lay the black paper on it. Put the water next to it. A grown-up holds the glass. Never look at the Sun.
flow.parent: The sun must fall straight on the plate, not through a closed window that is dusty or tinted. An open window or a balcony is best. If the sky is cloudy, try another day. Hazy sun works, but the paper takes longer to smoke. Keep children's fingers out from under the lens.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun Dot experiment. You gather sunlight with a magnifying glass and see what it does to paper.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess, and to give a reason, before anything is tried.
flow.say: Before we try anything, tell me your guess. When I hold the glass low, it makes a big circle of light. When I lift it, the circle shrinks to a tiny dot. What will each one do to the paper? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. What will the big circle do to the paper? What will the tiny dot do? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Will the tiny dot be hotter than the big circle? Why?
good: Yes, because all the light is squeezed into one small place.
I don't know, because it is the same sunlight.

flow.parent: Write the guess down. Many children think the lens makes the light stronger, or that the paper will catch fire at once. Both are fine guesses. Don't explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Hold the magnifying glass flat, about 2 cm above the black paper, so that a big circle of light lies on it. 2. Count to 60 out loud together. 3. Move the lens away. 4. Let your child touch the paper with one finger.
flow.say: This is the big circle. The glass is letting all its light through, but spread out. Let's count to 60 and watch. Now touch the paper. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Look at the big circle of light on the paper. Count to 60. Does it smoke? Now touch the paper. Is it warm?
flow.parent: Nothing should smoke. The paper will feel warm, about as warm as any black thing in the sun. Write 'no smoke in 60 seconds' in the table.

flow.do: 1. Slowly lift the glass until the circle shrinks to the smallest, brightest dot you can make. 2. Hold it still. 3. Count seconds until you see a thin thread of smoke. 4. Move the lens away at once and write the number. 5. Do it twice more, each time on a fresh part of the paper.
flow.say: Now I lift the glass slowly. Watch the circle shrink. Keep counting. Tell me the moment you see smoke. Now we try twice more, on fresh paper, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Watch the circle shrink to a tiny dot. Count the seconds. Shout when you see smoke! Then try two more times.

check.q: The big circle only warmed the black paper. The tiny dot made it smoke. What did the glass do?
options: It made extra light
It gathered the same light into a much smaller place
It dried the paper out
check.why: The magnifying glass made no new light. It took the sunlight falling on its whole face and packed it into a tiny dot. That dot got hundreds of times more light than plain sunshine. Picking 'made extra light' is a very common guess, but a lens cannot make light. Picking 'dried the paper' mixes up what we see. The paper got hot, and hot paper smokes.

flow.parent: With a 5 cm lens in strong sun, black paper usually smokes in about 2 to 10 seconds, and a small black hole appears. Glance at the dot, don't stare at it, even with sunglasses on. If nothing happens, the dot is probably not as small as it can be. Lift or lower the lens slightly. If it still does not smoke, the sun is too weak today.

flow.do: 1. Swap the black paper for the white paper. 2. Hold the glass at the same height, making the same tiny dot. 3. Count seconds until smoke, and stop at 60. 4. Try 3 times, on fresh spots.
flow.say: Now the white paper. Same glass, same dot, same sunshine. Only the paper has changed. Will it smoke sooner, later or not at all?
flow.kid: Now the white paper. Same glass. Same tiny dot. Count again. Stop at 60. Did it smoke?
flow.parent: White paper usually takes much longer, and often does not smoke at all within 60 seconds. It may turn brown first. The dot on white paper is very dazzling, so look only in short glances. If your white paper has printed words, a black letter will smoke first. That is a good extra result.

flow.do: 1. Pour water over both papers. 2. Take the magnifying glass indoors and put it in a drawer. 3. Look at the holes together.
flow.say: Let's make the paper safe, and put the glass away in a drawer. A lens left lying in the sun can start a fire on its own.
flow.kid: Pour water on the papers. Put the glass away in a drawer. Look at the little holes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.think: Your eye has a lens inside it too. What would it do with sunlight if you looked at the Sun?
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: sunlight smokes paper only when it is gathered into a small dot, and black paper gets hot faster than white. What I saw: the big circle never smoked in 60 seconds. The tiny dot made black paper smoke in about 4 seconds. White paper took over 30 seconds, or did not smoke. Why: the lens packed the light into a small place, and black paper absorbs more light than white.

experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up uses a magnifying glass to gather sunlight. You find out when sunlight is strong enough to make paper smoke, and whether the colour of the paper matters.

experiments.title: Ice on Black, Ice on White: which paper takes in more sunlight?
experiments.question: An ice cube sits on black paper, and another on white paper, in the same sunshine. Which melts first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which ice cube will melt first, the one on black paper or the one on white paper? Or will they melt at the same time? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two ice cubes from the same tray, two steel plates that are the same, and two sheets of paper the same size. Put both plates side by side in the same sunshine at the same moment. Only the colour of the paper changes.
results_table: What the ice looks like after 5 minutes

materials.item: two ice cubes from the same tray
a sheet of black chart paper, or paper coloured black with a crayon
a sheet of white paper the same size
two steel plates that are the same
a sunny balcony, windowsill or terrace
a clock or phone timer

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun. Steel plates in strong sun can get hot, so touch them only at the edge.

schedule.what: Put ice on black paper and white paper in the sun. Check every 5 minutes until both have melted.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both plates at 10 minutes, showing how big each ice cube is and how big each puddle is.

flow.do: 1. Lay one sheet of paper flat on each steel plate. 2. Put both plates side by side in direct sunshine. 3. Take two ice cubes from the freezer. Put one in the middle of each sheet at the same moment.
flow.say: Two ice cubes, from the same tray. Two plates, side by side, in the same sun. The only difference is the paper. Black under one, white under the other.
flow.kid: Put the black paper and the white paper in the sun, side by side. Put one ice cube on each, at the same time.
flow.parent: The paper will get wet, which is fine. On a hot day in direct sun, each cube may melt in about 15 to 30 minutes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ice test. You put an ice cube on black paper and another on white paper, in the same sunshine, to see which paper takes in more sunlight.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Which ice cube will melt first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which ice will melt first? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why might the colour of the paper matter, if the sunlight is the same?
good: Black things get hotter in the sun.
The black paper might take in more of the light.

flow.do: 1. Every 5 minutes, look at both cubes together. 2. Write down how big each cube is and how big its puddle is. 3. Gently touch each sheet near the edge with the back of a finger, and say which feels warmer.
flow.say: Five minutes. Let's look. Which cube is smaller? Which puddle is bigger? Touch the edge of each paper. Which one is warmer?
flow.kid: Every 5 minutes, look at both ice cubes. Which is smaller? Touch the edge of each paper. Which is warmer?
flow.parent: The cube on black paper should shrink faster and sit in a bigger puddle. The dry edge of the black paper will feel warmer. If clouds cover the Sun, both slow down. Keep going until the Sun comes back.

flow.do: Write down the minute each cube finishes melting.
flow.say: Which one melted first? How many minutes did each take?
flow.kid: Which ice melted first? Write the minutes for each.

check.q: The ice on black paper melted first. Why?
options: Black paper is made of warmer stuff
Black paper absorbs more sunlight, and the light turns into heat
The white paper made cold
check.why: Both sheets got the same sunlight. The black paper absorbed most of it, and the light turned into heat in the paper. The heat moved into the ice. The white paper reflected most of the light back, so it stayed cooler. Picking 'made cold' means thinking white makes coldness. It doesn't. It just takes in less of the Sun's energy.

flow.do: Ask for three things: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Tell me what you think now, what you saw, and why it happened.
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.think: Why do people in hot places often paint their roofs white?
flow.parent: A good answer: black paper takes in more sunlight than white paper. My ice on black melted in 18 minutes and the ice on white in 27 minutes, and the black paper felt warmer. The black paper absorbed the light and it turned into heat, which melted the ice.

activities.title: Sun Patch, Shade Patch: what does your skin notice?

materials.item: a patch of sunlight on the floor, from a window or balcony door

activities.safety: Keep your back or side to the Sun. Never look at it.

schedule.what: Stand in sunlight, then in shade. Feel the difference. Feel the floor in both places.

activities.record: Draw yourself half in the sunlight and half in the shade. Write one word for how each half felt.

flow.do: 1. Find a patch of sunlight on the floor. 2. Stand in it with your back to the window for one minute. 3. Step into the shade next to it for one minute.
flow.say: Stand in the sunlight with your back to the window. Wait a minute. Now step into the shade. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Stand in the sunlight, with your back to the window. Count to 60. Now step into the shade. What do you feel?

ask.q: Where did you feel warmer? Which part of you felt it most?
good: In the sunlight, on my back.
On my hair, because it is dark.

flow.context: This is a quick start for the Sun unit. You feel the difference between sunlight and shade, and wonder where the warmth comes from.

flow.do: Put your palm flat on the floor, first in the sunny patch, then in the shade.
flow.say: Now feel the floor in both places. Which part is warmer? The sunlight came through a window, from 150 million kilometres away.
flow.kid: Put your hand on the sunny floor. Then on the shady floor. Which is warmer?

check.q: The sunny floor is warmer than the shady floor. Where was the warmth made?
options: In the floor, when it absorbed the sunlight
In space, on the way from the Sun
In the window glass
check.why: Space is nearly empty, so there is almost nothing there to warm. The floor absorbed the sunlight, and the light turned into heat right there in the floor. Picking 'in space' is a natural guess, because the Sun is hot. But the light only becomes warmth when something absorbs it.

flow.do: Leave your child with a question.
flow.say: The sunlight felt gentle on your back. Could the same sunlight ever be strong enough to burn paper? We will find out.
flow.kid: The sunlight felt gentle. Could it ever burn paper? Keep that question in your head!
flow.think: What could make gentle sunlight strong enough to burn?

activities.context: This is a short way into the unit. You feel sunlight and shade with your skin and hand, and ask where the warmth comes from.

activities.title: The Mirror Sun: a safe picture of the Sun on your wall

materials.item: a small mirror, such as a pocket or handbag mirror
a piece of paper and tape, to cover the mirror
scissors
a window or balcony door with direct sun, and a shaded wall inside the room at least 3 metres away. A white or pale wall is best.
a measuring tape and a ruler

activities.safety: Never look into the mirror at the Sun. Never shine the reflected sunlight into anyone's eyes, or out of the window at people or vehicles. A grown-up helps with the scissors.

schedule.what: Cover a mirror, cut a small square hole, and reflect the Sun onto a far wall. Measure the round spot and how far away it is.

activities.record: Draw the square hole and the round spot. Write the spot's width and its distance from the mirror.

flow.do: 1. Tape paper over the whole mirror. 2. Cut a small square hole in the middle, about 1 cm wide.
flow.say: We will make a picture of the Sun that you can look at as long as you like. First we cover the mirror and cut a small square window in the paper.
flow.kid: Tape paper over the mirror. Cut a small square hole in the middle. A grown-up helps with the scissors.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Mirror Sun. You make a picture of the Sun on a wall, so that you can study the Sun without ever looking at it.

flow.do: 1. Stand in the sunshine at the window. 2. Tilt the mirror until a spot of reflected light lands on a shaded wall across the room. 3. Hold the mirror as still as you can, or rest it on the windowsill against a book.
flow.say: Tilt the mirror slowly. Find the spot of light on the far wall. What shape is it?
flow.kid: Stand in the sun with the mirror. Tilt it slowly. Find the spot of light on the far wall. What shape is it?

check.q: The hole in the paper is square, but the spot on the far wall is round. Why?
options: The wall bends the light
The spot is a picture of the round Sun
The mirror is round
check.why: A small hole lets through light from every part of the Sun. Far away, that light makes a picture of the Sun itself, and the Sun is round. Picking 'the mirror is round' is a good try, but the paper covers most of the mirror, and only the square hole lets light through. Try a triangle-shaped hole too: the far spot is still round.

flow.parent: The spot on a wall about 4 to 6 metres away is round. Close to the mirror, held up on a book, the spot is square, the shape of the hole. Move a sheet of paper slowly from the mirror towards the wall, catching the spot, and watch it change from square to round.

flow.do: 1. Measure the width of the round spot on the wall with a ruler. 2. Measure the distance from the mirror to the wall with the tape. 3. Write both numbers down in centimetres.
flow.say: Let's measure the spot, and how far it is from the mirror. Scientists measure pictures like this to work out how big the Sun looks from Earth.
flow.kid: Measure how wide the round spot is. Then measure from the mirror to the wall. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: On a wall 500 cm away, the spot is about 5 to 6 cm wide. Take away the width of the hole, 1 cm, and divide the distance by what is left. You should get roughly 100. That means the Sun is about 100 times further away than it is wide. The real number is about 108.

flow.do: Ask your child to look at the spot for as long as they like, and say what they notice.
flow.say: This spot is the real Sun's light, and it is safe to look at, because it is on a wall. What do you notice? Is it white or yellow?
flow.kid: You can look at this Sun as long as you like. Is it white or yellow? Does it wobble?
flow.think: Why is this picture safe to look at, when the real Sun is not?
flow.parent: The spot usually looks white, which is the Sun's real colour. It wobbles if the mirror moves. Large sunspots are too small to see with a 1 cm hole.

activities.title: What Has the Sun Changed? A home hunt

materials.item: a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Stay inside the home or on the balcony. Never look at the Sun.

schedule.what: Hunt around the home for things the Sun has warmed, dried, faded or made grow.

activities.record: Make a list with four headings: warmed, dried, faded, grown. Write each thing you find under one heading.

flow.do: Explain the hunt.
flow.say: The Sun leaves marks all over a home. Let's hunt for things it has warmed, dried, faded, or helped to grow.
flow.kid: Hunt for things the Sun has changed. Warmed. Dried. Faded. Grown. How many can you find?
flow.context: This is a hunt around the home for things sunlight has changed, which shows that sunlight carries energy.

flow.do: Walk round the home together. Look at curtains, posters near windows, old newspapers, clothes on the line, a balcony floor, and any plant by a window.
flow.say: Look at the curtain. Is the side facing the window paler? Feel the balcony floor. Which plants are by the window?
flow.kid: Look at the curtains. Is one side paler? Feel the balcony floor. Find a plant near the window.

ask.q: Why is the curtain paler on the side that faces the window?
good: Ultraviolet light in sunlight breaks down the colour.

ask.q: Why does the plant by the window need the sunlight?
good: She uses it to make her food.

flow.parent: Common finds: a curtain or cushion faded on one side, a yellowed newspaper, dry clothes, warm floor tiles, a plant leaning towards the window. If you can't find faded things, the next project shows the Sun fading paper over a few days.

flow.do: Count the finds under each heading.
flow.say: Every one of these needed energy. All of that energy came in through the window as sunlight.
flow.kid: Count your finds. Every one needed energy. It all came from the Sun.

check.q: Kavitha, a girl in Class 3, finds that her poster by the window has gone pale. What did that?
options: Sunlight, mostly the ultraviolet light in it
The cold air from the window
Dust from the road
check.why: Sunlight carries energy, and ultraviolet light, which we cannot see, has enough to break down the colours in paint and ink. That is why posters and curtains fade where the Sun reaches them. Picking 'dust' is a sensible guess, because dust makes things look dull. But dust can be wiped off, and fading cannot.

activities.title: The Sunbeam's Long Trip: act it out

materials.item: 6 to 10 cushions or pillows
a potted plant, a dark cloth and a white sheet of paper

activities.safety: Clear a space so nobody trips on the cushions.

schedule.what: Act out the journey of the Sun's energy from the core to the Earth.

activities.record: Draw the trip: a wiggly line inside the Sun and a straight line across space.

flow.do: 1. Pile the cushions close together at one end of the room. This is the inside of the Sun. 2. Put the plant, the dark cloth and the white paper at the other end. This is the Earth.
flow.say: These cushions are the packed insides of the Sun. Over there is the Earth. You are a bit of energy, just made in the Sun's core.
flow.kid: The cushions are the inside of the Sun. Over there is the Earth. You are a bit of energy from the core!
flow.context: This is an act-out of the journey that the Sun's energy makes, from the core to the Earth.

flow.do: Your child starts in the middle of the cushions. Each time they touch a cushion, they must turn and go a different way. They zigzag until they get out of the pile.
flow.say: Inside the Sun, you keep getting taken in and sent out again, in a new direction. Bump, turn, bump, turn. It takes many thousands of years to get out.
flow.kid: Start in the middle. Touch a cushion, then turn a new way. Keep zigzagging until you get out!
flow.parent: This shows why energy takes a very long time to leave the Sun. Scientists estimate between about 10,000 and 170,000 years.

flow.do: Once out, your child walks straight across the room to the Earth while everyone counts slowly to 8.
flow.say: Now you are sunlight in empty space. Nothing gets in your way. Walk straight to the Earth while we count 8 slow minutes.
flow.kid: Now walk straight to the Earth. We count to 8, for 8 minutes!

flow.do: Your child chooses where to land: on the plant, the dark cloth or the white paper. They act out what happens next.
flow.say: Where will you land? On the plant, you become her food. On the dark cloth, you turn into heat. On the white paper, you bounce off again.
flow.kid: Where will you land? The plant? The dark cloth? The white paper? Show what happens!

check.q: The sunbeam lands on the white paper. What happens to most of it?
options: It is reflected and bounces away
It all turns into heat
It disappears
check.why: White things reflect most of the light that falls on them, so most of the sunbeam bounces off. That is why white paper stays cooler than black paper in the sun. Picking 'disappears' is a natural guess, but energy is never lost. It always goes somewhere.

activities.context: This is an act-out. You play a bit of the Sun's energy, travelling from the core to the Earth.

setup.caption: 2. Walk straight across space to the Earth.

projects.title: The Sun Print: a picture made only by sunlight

materials.item: a sheet of coloured paper that fades easily, such as kite paper, tissue paper or cheap coloured craft paper. A sheet of newspaper works too.
3 or 4 flat objects with clear shapes: a key, a coin, a leaf, a cut-out cardboard star
a piece of clear glass from an old photo frame, or clear plastic, to hold everything flat
a windowsill or balcony ledge that gets several hours of direct sun each day

projects.safety: A grown-up handles the glass and checks it has no sharp edges. Put the print where it cannot fall.

schedule.what: Lay the objects on the paper, cover with glass, and put it in the sun. Draw what it looks like.
Look without moving anything. Is the paper around the objects changing colour?
Lift off the glass and the objects. Look at the shapes left behind. Explain what made them.

projects.record: Draw the print on day 1 and on day 6. Write which parts changed and which did not.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper on a flat piece of cardboard. 2. Lay the objects on it, spaced apart. 3. Cover with the glass or clear plastic. 4. Put it in a spot that gets direct sun for several hours.
flow.say: We will let the Sun draw a picture for us. The objects will block the sunlight. Let's see what the uncovered paper looks like in a few days.
flow.kid: Lay the key, coin and leaf on the paper. Cover them with the glass. Put it all in the sun.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to the paper that is in the sun?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Sun Print, a 6-day project. The Sun's ultraviolet light slowly fades paper, except where something blocks it.

flow.do: On day 3, look at the print without moving anything.
flow.say: Don't lift anything yet. Can you see the paper changing colour around the objects?
flow.kid: Look, but don't touch! Is the paper changing colour?
flow.wait: Leave it in the sun until day 3.
flow.parent: Kite paper and tissue fade fastest. Newspaper turns slightly yellow. If nothing has changed by day 3, leave it longer, or move it to a sunnier spot.

flow.do: On day 6, lift off the glass and the objects. Look at the shapes.
flow.say: Now lift everything off. What did the Sun draw? Why are the shapes a different colour from the rest?
flow.kid: Lift off the glass. Lift off the key and coin. What did the Sun draw?
flow.wait: Leave it in the sun until day 6.

check.q: The paper under the key kept its colour. The paper around it faded. Why?
options: The key blocked the sunlight, so no ultraviolet light reached that paper
The key was cold
The key's metal coloured the paper
check.why: Sunlight, mostly its ultraviolet part, breaks down the colour in the paper. The key is opaque, so it blocked the light, and the paper under it kept its colour. Picking 'the key's metal coloured the paper' is a good thought, but the leaf and the cardboard star leave the same kind of shape, and they are not metal.

challenges.title: Melt the Chocolate with Only Sunlight
challenges.problem: Build a sun cooker from a cardboard box that melts a piece of chocolate as fast as possible, using only sunlight.
constraints: No flame, no electricity, and no magnifying glass.
Put a piece of chocolate in a small steel bowl inside your cooker, and time how long it takes to melt.
materials: a cardboard box, such as a shoebox
clear plastic wrap or a clear plastic bag
a small steel bowl and two small pieces of chocolate, the same size
general: Line the inside of the box with foil, so it reflects sunlight onto the bowl.
Put black paper under the bowl, so it absorbs the light and gets hot.
Cover the top with clear plastic, so sunlight gets in but the warm air stays in.
creative: Make foil-covered flaps that open out from the top of the box, like petals, to catch more sunlight and reflect it in.
Mária Telkes, a scientist known as the Sun Queen, designed simple sun ovens for families in the 1950s. Look up a picture of one and borrow an idea.
Turn the box every 15 minutes to face the Sun as it moves across the sky.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own sun cooker. Draw it, build it, and race it against a piece of chocolate left in a bowl in the open sun. Which melts first?

flow.do: Put one piece of chocolate in a steel bowl in the open sun. This is the one to beat.
flow.say: This chocolate is in plain sunshine. Can we build something that melts chocolate faster, with no flame and no magnifying glass?
flow.kid: Put one piece of chocolate in a bowl in the sun. Can you build a box that melts chocolate faster?
flow.context: This is the first step of the sun cooker challenge. You build a box that gathers sunlight to melt chocolate.

flow.do: Build the cooker. Use foil to reflect light in, black paper to absorb it, and plastic to keep the warm air in.
flow.say: Think about what you have learned. Foil reflects light. Black absorbs it. How can you send more sunlight onto the bowl, and keep the heat in?
flow.kid: Build your cooker. Foil sends light in. Black paper soaks it up. Plastic keeps the heat in.
flow.parent: Help with the scissors. Any design that reflects light into the box and absorbs it on black paper should beat the open bowl.

flow.do: Put the second piece of chocolate in a bowl in the cooker, in the sun. Check both every 5 minutes.
flow.say: Let's race. Which chocolate goes soft first?
flow.kid: Put the second chocolate in your cooker. Check both every 5 minutes. Which melts first?

check.q: Why does foil inside the box help the chocolate melt faster?
options: Foil reflects extra sunlight onto the bowl
Foil makes heat by itself
Foil keeps the light out
check.why: Shiny foil reflects most of the light that falls on it. Angled the right way, it sends extra sunlight onto the bowl. Picking 'makes heat by itself' is a common mix-up: foil makes no heat. It only sends light to where the black paper and the bowl can absorb it.

flow.do: Talk about what worked best, and what you would change.
flow.say: What worked best? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: What worked best? What would you change?

challenges.title: An Eclipse Party for the Whole Building
challenges.problem: A solar eclipse is coming, and 30 people in your building want to watch it. Only one family has eclipse glasses. Plan a way for everyone to see the eclipse safely, at the same time, without anyone looking at the Sun.
constraints: Nobody may look straight at the Sun, even for a second.
Small children must be able to see it too.
materials: a steel colander or a sieve
cardboard and foil, for pinhole viewers
a white bedsheet or white chart paper
general: Hold a colander in the sunlight above white paper. Every hole makes a tiny picture of the Sun, so everyone sees many little eclipses at once.
Use covered mirrors to throw pictures of the Sun onto a shaded wall, as in the Mirror Sun.
Make pinhole viewers from cardboard and foil, one for each family.
creative: Hang a white bedsheet in a shaded stairwell and use a covered mirror to throw a big Sun picture onto it for everyone.
Poke holes in a sheet of card to spell a word. During the eclipse, each hole makes a little crescent Sun.
Ask everyone to bring a colander, and compare the patterns.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own eclipse party. Draw where people stand, what they look at, and what the grown-ups must watch out for.

flow.do: Read the problem together.
flow.say: Thirty people, one pair of eclipse glasses. How can everyone watch the eclipse safely?
flow.kid: Thirty people want to watch an eclipse. There is one pair of eclipse glasses. How can everyone see safely?
flow.context: This is the first step of the eclipse party challenge. You plan how a whole building can watch an eclipse without anyone looking at the Sun.

flow.do: On a sunny day, test a colander over white paper, and the Mirror Sun.
flow.say: Let's test two ideas today. Hold the colander in the sun above the paper. What do you see?
flow.kid: Hold the colander in the sun above white paper. What do you see on the paper?

check.q: Under a colander in the sun, each hole makes a small round spot. What is each spot?
options: A tiny picture of the Sun
A shadow of the colander
A reflection of the sky
check.why: Each small hole works like a pinhole and makes its own little picture of the Sun. During an eclipse, every spot becomes a little crescent. Picking 'a shadow' is close: the dark part is the colander's shadow, but the bright spots are pictures of the Sun.

flow.parent: Today the spots will be round. During a partial eclipse they turn into crescents, like a bitten biscuit.

flow.do: Draw the plan: where people stand, what they use, and who keeps watch.
flow.say: Now draw your plan. Who keeps an eye on the small children? Where does the mirror picture go?
flow.kid: Draw your plan. Where do people stand? Who watches the little children?

flow.do: Share the plan with a neighbour or with the family.
flow.say: Explain your plan to someone, and tell them why looking at the Sun is never safe.
flow.kid: Tell someone your plan. Tell them why we never look at the Sun.
