quiz.p: The Sun looks much bigger and brighter than the stars at night. Why?
opts: It is the biggest star there is
It is much closer to us than any other star
quiz.why: The Sun is an ordinary star that happens to be very close. The next nearest star is about 270,000 times further away. Picking 'the biggest star' is a natural guess, but many stars are much bigger.

quiz.p: What is the Sun mostly made of?
opts: Hydrogen, with most of the rest helium
quiz.why: The Sun is mostly hydrogen, the lightest kind of atom, and most of the rest is helium. Picking 'rock and iron' means thinking of the Sun as being like the Earth. People thought so until 1925.

quiz.p: How does the Sun make its light?
opts: By joining hydrogen into helium in its core
By reflecting light from other stars
quiz.why: In the core, hydrogen joins into helium, and a tiny bit of material turns into energy. This is nuclear fusion. Picking 'by shrinking' was a real idea in the 1800s, but it would have used up the Sun in a few tens of millions of years.

quiz.p: Selvi, a girl in Class 3, says a fire as big as the Sun would still be burning today. Why is she wrong?
opts: A fire that big would have burnt out in a few thousand years
The Sun is colder than a fire
quiz.why: A ball of coal as big as the Sun would burn out in a few thousand years, and it would need oxygen, which space does not have. The Sun has shone for about 4.6 billion years.

quiz.p: Two steel plates stand in the sun, one with black paper and one with white paper. Which paper gets warmer?
quiz.why: Black paper absorbs most of the sunlight, and the light turns into heat. White paper reflects most of it. Picking 'both the same' makes sense, because the sunlight is the same. But what the paper does with it is different.

quiz.p: Where does sunlight turn into heat?
opts: In empty space on the way
quiz.why: Sunlight turns into heat where it is absorbed: on your skin, a road, a leaf or black paper. Empty space has almost nothing to absorb it.

quiz.p: A magnifying glass makes a big circle of light on black paper, then a tiny dot. Which makes the paper smoke?
quiz.why: The tiny dot has all the light from the glass packed into a small place, so it gets hot enough to smoke. The big circle spreads it out.

quiz.p: In the Sun Dot experiment, why was the paper put on a steel plate, with a tumbler of water nearby?
opts: To keep it safe, so nothing else could catch fire
quiz.why: Steel does not burn, and the water can put out any smouldering paper. The steel plate and the water are there for safety. A grown-up holds the glass for the same reason.

quiz.p: Why can looking at the Sun harm your eyes without any pain?
opts: The retina has no pain nerves
quiz.why: The eye's lens focuses the Sun's light onto the retina, which has no pain nerves. So the harm happens without warning, and may show only later. That is why we never look at the Sun.

quiz.p: Which of these is a safe way to watch the Sun?
opts: Its picture on a wall, made by a covered mirror
A quick look for one second
quiz.why: A picture of the Sun on a wall is safe, because you look at the wall, not the Sun. Sunglasses let through too much light, binoculars gather more of it into the eye, and even one second can harm the retina.

quiz.p: Why does a garden lizard lie on a sunny wall in the cool early morning?
opts: To warm her body, so she can move fast and hunt
quiz.why: A lizard makes little heat inside her own body. On a cool morning she is slow. Basking lets her absorb sunlight and warm up, so she can chase insects.

quiz.p: In 1920, Arthur Eddington suggested how the Sun shines. What new measurement helped him?
opts: That a helium atom weighs a little less than four hydrogen atoms
That the Sun is full of coal
That sunlight takes 8 minutes to arrive
quiz.why: Francis Aston measured that a helium atom weighs a little less than four hydrogen atoms. Eddington saw that if the Sun joins hydrogen into helium, the missing material could become the Sun's energy.

items.p: What kind of thing is the Sun?
items.why: The Sun is a star, a huge ball of very hot gas that makes its own light. It is the nearest star to the Earth. Picking 'a ball of fire' is very common, but the Sun does not burn. It shines by fusion. A strong answer says it is the nearest star.

items.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3, says, 'The Sun is a giant fire, burning in the sky.' Is she right?
items.why: False. A fire needs oxygen from the air, and there is no air in space. The Sun shines because hydrogen joins into helium in its core. A strong answer gives this reason.

items.p: A thing that takes in light, so that the light turns into heat, is said to ____ the light.
items.why: Absorb means take in. Black things absorb most of the light that falls on them, so they get hot in the sun.

items.p: Remember the Sun Dot experiment, where a grown-up held a magnifying glass over black paper in the sun. When did the paper smoke?
opts: When the glass made a big circle of light
When the glass made a tiny dot of light
items.why: The tiny dot had all the light from the whole glass packed into a small place, so it got hot enough to smoke. The big circle spread the light out, so it only warmed the paper. A strong answer says the lens gathered the light.

items.p: In the Sun Dot experiment, the glass made no new light, but the tiny dot made paper smoke. Explain how.
items.a: The magnifying glass gathered all the sunlight that fell on it into one tiny dot. The same amount of light was packed into a much smaller place, so that spot of paper got very hot.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of gathering or focusing, and says the amount of light stayed the same but the place got smaller.

items.p: Why must we never look straight at the Sun?
opts: The Sun is too far away to see
The lens in our eye focuses its light onto the retina and harms it
items.why: The eye's lens gathers light like a magnifying glass. Looking at the Sun focuses its light into a tiny fierce spot on the retina, which can be harmed for ever. A strong answer names the lens and the retina.

items.p: Lalitha, a girl in Class 3 in Mysuru, wants to watch the Sun. Sort these ways: safe or not safe?
items: a picture of the Sun on a wall, made by a covered mirror
Safe
ordinary sunglasses
Not safe
little suns under a colander
Safe
binoculars
Not safe
eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2
Safe
a quick look for one second
Not safe
items.a: see items
items.why: The safe ways make a picture of the Sun to look at, or use a filter made for the Sun. Sunglasses let through far too much light. Binoculars gather even more light into the eye. Even one second can harm the retina. A strong answer sorts by whether light from the Sun goes straight into the eye.

items.p: Draw a magnifying glass above a sheet of paper in the sun. Draw the lines of sunlight going through the glass and meeting in a tiny dot on the paper.
items.a: Straight lines of sunlight coming down, bending as they pass through the glass, and meeting at one point on the paper.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the light from the whole glass ends up in one small spot.
items.art: A blank box with a small Sun drawn in the top corner.

items.p: Remember the ice test, with one ice cube on black paper and one on white paper in the sun. Which melted first?
opts: Both at exactly the same time
Neither, ice cannot melt in sunlight
items.why: Black paper absorbs more sunlight than white paper, and the light turns into heat in the paper. That heat melted the ice faster. White paper reflects most of the light. A strong answer uses the words absorb and reflect.

items.p: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to the Earth.
items.why: True. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres away, and light crosses that in about 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a huge ball of hot gas that makes its own light
clear curved glass that bends light
the light-catching layer at the back of the eye
the centre of the Sun, where its energy is made
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.

items.p: Label the drawing of a cut-open eye looking at the Sun: lens, retina, and the spot where the Sun's light meets.
items.a: The lens near the front of the eye, the retina lining the back, and a dot on the retina where the lines of light meet.
items.why: The lens gathers light onto the retina. A strong label shows the meeting spot on the retina, the place that is harmed.
items.art: A side view of an eye with lines of sunlight entering from the left, and three blank label lines.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
opts: Sirius, the brightest star at night
items.why: The Sun, Sirius and the Pole Star are all stars, which make their own light. The Moon is not a star. It shines only because it reflects sunlight.

items.p: Remember the Sunbeam Race, where you travelled from the Sun's core to the Earth. You land on a black road. What happens to you?
opts: You are absorbed and turn into heat
items.why: A black road absorbs most of the sunlight that lands on it, and the light turns into heat. That is why a road in summer is too hot for bare feet.

items.p: A garden lizard lies flat on a sunny wall early in the morning. What problem does she have on a cool morning, and how does the sunshine help her?
items.a: Her body does not make much heat of its own, so on a cool morning she is slow and cannot chase insects well. Lying flat in the sun, she absorbs sunlight, warms up, and can then move fast and hunt.
items.why: A strong answer says the lizard's own problem first, being cold and slow, and then how basking solves it.

items.p: Two friends in Kochi are talking about the Sun.

views.says: The Sun can't be dangerous. Its light feels gentle and warm on my hands.
The Sun is very dangerous. A magnifying glass made its light burn paper.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Sun Dot experiment. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer says both are partly right. Spread-out sunlight on the skin is gentle for a short time, as Anjana says, though it can still burn skin over a long time. Gathered by a lens, the same light is fierce enough to burn paper, as Rehana saw. The eye has a lens, so looking at the Sun is dangerous, even though sunlight on the hands is not.
items.why: This tests the main idea of the unit: how strong sunlight is depends on how much is gathered into one place.

items.p: Sumathi's magnifying glass made black paper smoke in 4 seconds. She tried again with a bigger magnifying glass, held to make an equally tiny dot. What do you predict?
opts: It will take longer, because the glass is heavier
It will smoke faster, because a bigger glass gathers more sunlight into the dot
items.why: A bigger glass catches more sunlight across its face, and packs it into the dot. More light in the same small place means more heat, so the paper smokes faster. A strong answer explains with the amount of light caught.

items.p: In the Sun Dot experiment, white paper took much longer to smoke than black paper, under the same dot. Explain why.
items.a: White paper reflects most of the light that falls on it, so only a little turns into heat. Black paper absorbs most of the light, so it gets hot much faster.
items.why: A strong answer uses the words reflect and absorb, and says that the light was the same for both papers.

items.p: Arun says, 'If I wear two pairs of sunglasses, I can look at the Sun safely.' What is wrong with his idea?
opts: Nothing, two pairs are dark enough
Even two pairs let through far too much light, and the retina gives no warning
items.why: Sunglasses are made to cut glare, not to block the Sun's full light. Even two pairs let through far too much. The retina has no pain nerves, so Arun would feel nothing while it was harmed. Only eclipse glasses made for the Sun are safe.

items.p: A solar eclipse sends out special harmful rays that the Sun does not send on other days.
items.why: False. The Sun's light is just as harmful on any day. During an eclipse, the sky is darker, so the pupils open wider, and people stare for longer. That is why more eyes are harmed then.

items.p: Put the journey of the Sun's energy in order.
items: It crosses space in about 8 minutes
It is made when hydrogen joins into helium in the core
It lands on a leaf, and the plant uses the light's energy to make food
It works its way out through the packed inside of the Sun for thousands of years
a: It is made when hydrogen joins into helium in the core
It works its way out through the packed inside of the Sun for thousands of years
It crosses space in about 8 minutes
It lands on a leaf, and the plant uses the light's energy to make food
items.why: Energy is made in the core, takes thousands of years to reach the surface, crosses space in minutes, and is then absorbed on Earth.

items.p: Remember the Mirror Sun, where a covered mirror made a picture of the Sun on a wall. The hole in the paper was square. What shape was the spot on the far wall?
items.why: Far from the mirror, the spot is a picture of the Sun, so it is round whatever the shape of the hole. Close to the mirror it is square. A strong answer says the spot is a picture of the Sun.

items.p: People in Chennai often paint their roofs white to keep their rooms cooler in summer. Explain why this works.
items.a: White paint reflects most of the sunlight that falls on it. So less light is absorbed by the roof and turned into heat, and less heat gets into the rooms below.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the ice test showed: white absorbs less sunlight than black.

items.p: Sort each part of sunlight by what it does.
cats: We feel it as warmth, but cannot see it
It fades colours and burns skin, but we cannot see it
items: visible light, the colours of the rainbow
We see it
infrared light
We feel it as warmth, but cannot see it
ultraviolet light
It fades colours and burns skin, but we cannot see it
items.a: see items
items.why: Sunlight is more than the light we see. Infrared lies beyond red, and ultraviolet beyond violet. A strong answer gives an example of each, such as warmth on the skin or a faded curtain.

items.p: Draw the Sun cut in half like an orange. Show the core in the middle, a wiggly path for the energy getting out, and a straight arrow from the surface to a small Earth.
items.a: A circle with a small centre labelled core, a zigzag line from the core to the edge, and a straight arrow from the edge to a small Earth, labelled 8 minutes.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the trip inside the Sun is slow and zigzag, while the trip across space is straight and fast.

items.p: Why can the Sun shine in space, where there is no air, when a fire cannot?
opts: The Sun carries its own air
The Sun shines by fusion, which needs no oxygen
The Sun is not really shining
items.why: A fire needs oxygen. The Sun's light comes from hydrogen joining into helium in its core, and that needs no oxygen at all. Picking 'carries its own air' mixes up the Sun with a rocket, which really does carry its own oxygen.

items.p: Plants make their food from sunlight, water and air. This is called ____.
items.why: Photosynthesis is how plants catch sunlight's energy. Almost every animal, including you, lives on food that plants made this way.

items.p: In the Sun Print project, a key lay on coloured paper in the sun for 6 days. What did the paper look like when the key was lifted?
opts: A key shape in the old bright colour, with faded paper around it
items.why: The key blocked the sunlight, so the paper under it kept its colour. The rest faded, mostly from ultraviolet light. A strong answer says the key blocked the light.

items.p: A family in Madurai is arguing about how to watch a coming solar eclipse.

views.says: Stay indoors with the curtains shut. It is not worth any risk.
Let's watch it with a colander and a mirror picture. Then nobody looks at the Sun.
I'll just look quickly through my sunglasses.

items.ask: Whose plan would you choose? Explain why using what you know about the eye. Then say what is sensible about one of the other plans.
items.a: A strong answer picks Kavya's plan, because the colander and the mirror make pictures of the Sun, so no sunlight is gathered into anyone's eye. It explains that sunglasses let through far too much light, and the retina has no pain nerves to give a warning, so the uncle's plan is dangerous. It also gives the grandmother her due: staying indoors is completely safe, and she is right to take the risk seriously, though the family would miss the eclipse.
items.why: There is a real choice between being completely safe and seeing the eclipse safely. Only the uncle's plan is truly harmful.

items.p: Many people think the Sun must be the biggest star there is, because it looks so big. How could you explain to them why it looks so big?
items.a: The Sun looks big only because it is so much closer than the other stars. Many stars are much bigger than the Sun, but they are so far away that they look like tiny dots.
items.why: A strong answer says that distance changes how big a thing looks, and gives an example, such as a building that looks tiny from far away.

items.p: Match each living thing to how they use the Sun.
pairs: catches sunlight to make her food
basks to warm her body before hunting
makes vitamin D in the skin with a little sunlight
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each living thing uses sunlight to solve their own problem: food, warmth, or strong bones.

items.p: Your eye's lens focuses the Sun's light onto the retina, but the retina has no pain nerves. Why does that make looking at the Sun even more dangerous?
items.a: If the retina could feel pain, you would look away at once, as you pull your hand away from a hot pan. Because it has no pain nerves, nothing warns you, and you can keep looking while it is being harmed, and you only find out later, when part of what you see is blurred or dark.
items.why: A strong answer compares it with a part of the body that feels pain, and says that pain is a warning.

items.p: Farida's magnifying glass is 5 cm across. It packs its sunlight into a dot 1 mm across. Her friend says the dot gets the same amount of light as a 1 mm patch of plain sunshine. What is wrong?
opts: The dot gets all the light that fell on the whole glass, far more than a 1 mm patch
The dot gets less light than a 1 mm patch
The glass makes the light colder
items.why: The glass catches the sunlight falling on its whole 5 cm face and sends it all into the 1 mm dot. That is hundreds of times more light than a 1 mm patch of plain sunshine gets. A strong answer compares the size of the glass with the size of the dot.

items.p: Lord Kelvin worked out that the Sun had probably not shone for 100 million years. Geologists said the Earth's rocks were much older. Who turned out to be right, and what did Kelvin not know about?
items.a: The geologists were right. Kelvin did not know about nuclear fusion, joining hydrogen into helium, which gives the Sun enough energy to shine for billions of years.
items.why: A strong answer says that a calculation can be careful and still wrong if it misses something nobody knew about yet.

items.p: Meenakshi left a glass bottle full of water on a sunny windowsill, next to a pile of old newspapers. Why is this a risk?
opts: The bottle can act as a lens and gather sunlight into a hot spot on the paper
items.why: A round bottle of water is thicker in the middle, like a lens. It can gather sunlight into a hot spot. On paper, that spot can smoulder and start a fire. Fires have really started this way.

items.p: In the ice test, Divya's two ice cubes melted at the same time. Suggest two reasons why her result came out differently from yours.
items.a: The sky may have been cloudy, so there was little sunlight for either paper to absorb. Or the plates may have been in the shade, or the papers may have been of very similar colours. One cube may also have been bigger.
items.why: A strong answer thinks about what makes the test fair, and about whether there was enough sunlight to make a difference.

items.p: If the Sun suddenly stopped shining, the Earth would go dark at that same moment.
items.why: False. The last light to leave the Sun would still be on its way. It takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so we would see the Sun for about 8 more minutes.

items.p: On a clear day the Sun looks pale yellow. At sunset over the sea, it looks orange. In space, it looks white. What causes the change?
opts: The Sun changes colour during the day
Our air scatters away blue light, and at sunset the light passes through much more air
The sea paints the Sun orange
items.why: The Sun's light is white. Air scatters blue light more than other colours. At sunset the light crosses much more air, so even more blue and green are scattered away, leaving orange and red. A strong answer mentions how much air the light passes through.

items.p: Space between the Sun and the Earth is nearly empty. Explain why sunlight does not warm up empty space, but does warm up your skin.
items.a: Sunlight turns into heat only when something absorbs it. Empty space has almost nothing in it to absorb the light, so it passes straight through. Your skin absorbs the light, so the light turns into heat there.
items.why: This is the puzzle from the start of the unit. A strong answer says heat appears where light is absorbed.

items.p: Put these in order, from the one that gets most sunlight onto one spot to the one that gets least.
items: a small piece of black paper in plain sunshine
a tiny dot made by a big magnifying glass
a tiny dot made by a small magnifying glass
a piece of black paper in the shade
a: a tiny dot made by a big magnifying glass
a tiny dot made by a small magnifying glass
a small piece of black paper in plain sunshine
a piece of black paper in the shade
items.why: A bigger glass gathers more light into its dot. Plain sunshine is not gathered at all. Shade gets the least. A strong answer explains the order with how much light is gathered.

items.p: Three people are talking about solar panels on the roof of their building in Hyderabad.

views.says: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity, and they give out no smoke. Every roof should have them.

views.who: Mrs Rao, who lives on the top floor
views.says: The roof is the only place where I can dry my clothes and vadams. Panels would take that away.
Panels cost a lot of money to put in. It takes years for them to pay for themselves.

items.ask: What would you advise the building to do? Use what you know about sunlight's energy. Then answer one of the other people fairly.
items.a: A strong answer uses the idea that sunlight carries a lot of energy, which panels can turn into electricity without smoke. It takes the other views seriously: it might suggest putting panels on raised frames so the roof below can still be used, or covering only part of the roof, and it accepts that the cost is real but is paid back over the years.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Clean electricity, space for daily life, and cost all matter, and a good answer weighs them.

items.p: Design a poster for your building telling children three safe ways to watch a solar eclipse. Draw each way.
items.a: Three clear drawings, such as a colander making little suns on paper, a covered mirror making a Sun picture on a wall, and a child wearing eclipse glasses marked ISO 12312-2, with the words 'Never look at the Sun'.
items.why: A strong poster shows ways where nobody looks straight at the Sun, and says why in one short line.

items.p: In the Mirror Sun, Lakshmi's round spot was 5 cm wide on a wall 500 cm away. What does 500 divided by 5 tell her?
opts: The Sun is about 100 times further away than it is wide
The Sun is 100 times bigger than the Earth
The mirror is 100 times too small
items.why: The spot is a picture of the Sun. The picture's width and distance are in the same proportion as the Sun's real width and distance. So the Sun is about 100 times further away than it is wide. Scientists measure about 108.

items.p: A plant on a dark shelf grows long and pale. Describe the plant's problem, and how growing long might help her.
items.a: The plant needs sunlight to make her food, and on a dark shelf she is not getting enough. Growing long stretches her towards wherever there might be more light, so she has a chance of reaching it.
items.why: A strong answer starts with the plant's own problem, needing light for food, and then explains how her growth helps.

items.p: In the Sun's core, hydrogen joins to make ____, and the missing bit of material becomes energy.
items.why: This is nuclear fusion. Arthur Eddington suggested it in 1920, after Francis Aston found that a helium atom weighs a little less than four hydrogen atoms.

items.p: Label the drawing of the Sun Dot experiment: magnifying glass, sunlight, the tiny dot, black paper, steel plate.
items.a: Sunlight coming from the top, the magnifying glass in the middle, lines meeting at the tiny dot on the black paper, and the steel plate underneath.
items.why: A strong label shows that the light from the whole glass meets at one dot.
items.art: A side-view drawing of a hand holding a lens over paper on a plate, with five blank label lines.

open_questions.q: Why is the Sun's outer layer, the corona, far hotter than its surface?
open_questions.why_open: The surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius, but the thin corona above it is over a million degrees. Scientists have several ideas, involving the Sun's magnetism, and spacecraft such as Aditya-L1 and NASA's Parker Solar Probe are testing them.

open_questions.q: Exactly how long does the Sun's energy take to get from the core to the surface?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody can see inside the Sun. Models give answers from about 10,000 to about 170,000 years.

open_questions.q: Can we forecast the Sun's storms days ahead, like rain?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can now give some warning of big solar storms, but they cannot yet say reliably which dark spot will erupt, or when.

open_questions.q: Where are the Sun's brothers and sisters?
open_questions.why_open: The Sun was probably born in a crowd of stars from the same cloud of gas, about 4.6 billion years ago. Those stars have since drifted apart, and astronomers are still trying to find them.

open_questions.q: Could we ever make fusion work on Earth, to make electricity like the Sun does?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists in many countries, including India, are building fusion machines. Some have made fusion happen for short times, but none yet gives out more useful energy than it takes to run.

maths.problem: In the Sun Dot experiment, the tiny dot made black paper smoke in 4 seconds. On white paper, the same dot took 40 seconds. How many times as long did the white paper take?
maths.explain: The white paper took 40 seconds and the black paper took 4 seconds. 40 divided by 4 is 10. So the white paper took 10 times as long. Check: 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 40.
maths.context: This is about the Sun Dot experiment. A grown-up holds a magnifying glass to make a tiny dot of sunlight, and you count the seconds until the paper smokes.

chart.title: Seconds until the paper smoked (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'white took longer' is true, but dividing tells us how much longer, which shows how big a difference the colour makes.

maths.problem: In the Mirror Sun, Lakshmi's round spot of light was 5 cm wide. The wall was 500 cm from the mirror. 500 divided by 5 is 100. What does that tell her about the real Sun?
maths.answer: The Sun is about 100 times further away than it is wide.
maths.explain: The picture of the Sun and the real Sun are in the same proportion. The picture is 100 times further from the mirror than it is wide. So the Sun is about 100 times further from us than it is wide. Scientists measure about 108, so her answer is close.
maths.context: This is about the Mirror Sun. You cover a mirror with paper, cut a small hole, and throw a picture of the Sun onto a far wall.
maths.why_maths: We can't put a ruler on the Sun. Dividing two measurements we can make at home tells us something true about the Sun itself.

maths.problem: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach the Earth. How many seconds is that?
maths.explain: 1 minute is 60 seconds. 8 minutes is 8 × 60 = 480 seconds. Add the 20 extra seconds: 480 + 20 = 500 seconds.
maths.context: This is about the journey of sunlight across space, from the Sun's surface to the Earth.
maths.why_maths: Changing minutes into seconds lets us compare the light's trip with things we can count, like the 4 seconds the paper took to smoke.

maths.problem: About 109 Earths fit in a line across the Sun's face. If each Earth were a 1 cm bead, how long would the line of beads be? Is that more or less than a metre?
maths.answer: 109 cm, which is a little more than a metre.
maths.explain: Each bead is 1 cm. 109 beads in a line make 109 cm. A metre is 100 cm. 109 is 9 more than 100, so the line is 9 cm longer than a metre.
maths.context: This is about how big the Sun is compared with the Earth.
maths.why_maths: A big number like 109 is hard to picture. Turning it into a line of beads you could lay on the floor shows the size.

maths.problem: In the ice test, Revathi's ice on black paper melted in 18 minutes. Her ice on white paper melted in 27 minutes. Then she tried grey paper. Predict how long the ice on grey paper might take, and explain your guess.
maths.answer: Somewhere between 18 and 27 minutes, perhaps about 22 minutes.
maths.explain: Grey is between black and white. It should absorb more sunlight than white but less than black. So its ice should melt faster than on white but slower than on black: between 18 and 27 minutes. Halfway is 22 and a half minutes, but the real time depends on how dark the grey is.
maths.context: This is about the ice test. You put an ice cube on black paper and another on white paper in the sun, and time how long each takes to melt.

chart.title: Minutes until the ice melted (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Using two results to predict a third, and then testing it, is how scientists check whether they really understand a pattern.

roots.context: We have learned what the Sun is, how its light turns into heat, and why a lens can make it fierce. Now we ask what the Sun's light tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Under the lens, black paper smoked in seconds, though the sunlight on it had only felt warm. The lens made no light. It gathered the light already falling on it into one dot. The lens in your eye gathers sunlight the same way, onto a spot that has no pain nerves.
deep_truth.habit: We judge whether something is harmful by how it feels. Sunlight feels gentle, so it seems safe. But how strong light is depends on how tightly it is gathered, and the spot in the eye where it is gathered has no pain nerves.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sun Dot experiment, the big circle of light never made the paper smoke in 60 seconds. The tiny dot made from the same light did it in a few seconds. Nothing was added. The light was only packed into a smaller place.

three.who_am_i: Your skin, your eyes and your food all take in sunlight. Part of you is always catching the Sun.
three.what_is_life: Almost every living thing runs on sunlight caught by plants, and a lizard on a wall warms up in the sunshine to start her day.
three.what_is_this_world: The Sun is one star among billions. The Earth catches only a tiny share of its light, and that share warms the whole world.

roots.thread: All the Sun's light starts in one small place, its core. From there it spreads out in every direction, across space. When it lands, it becomes many different things: warmth on your back, food in a leaf, a dry vadam, a faded curtain. A lens shows that the same light can be gentle or fierce, depending only on how much of it meets in one spot. One source becomes all these things, without ever changing what it is.

teachings.teaching: Just as a long road runs between two villages, the rays of the Sun run between the Sun and us. They start from the Sun and enter into the channels of the body.
teachings.link: Science agrees that sunlight really does enter us. Our skin absorbs it as warmth, our eyes catch it on the retina, and our food is made from it.

teachings.teaching: The Sun is new each day.
teachings.link: Every moment, the Sun's core turns about 4 million tonnes of material into energy. The light reaching you today is not yesterday's light. It is new light, made from the Sun itself.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, The Heart of Understanding (1988)
teachings.teaching: If you look deeply into a sheet of paper, you can see the sunshine in it. Without sunshine, the forest cannot grow, and without the forest there is no paper.
teachings.link: The paper in the Sun Dot experiment was made from trees that grew with sunlight. In the experiment, sunlight met paper made from sunlight.

other_view.view: Sunlight is energy. It turns into heat in a leaf or a sheet of paper because of how atoms absorb light, not because the Sun gives anything to anyone. Calling it a gift or a road into the body is a lovely picture, but it adds nothing to the physics.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat today. The Sun Dot needs direct sun, so it says to use a balcony, terrace or open window between about 10 and 3, and to wait for another day if it is cloudy. A grown-up holds the lens in every step, the paper sits on a steel plate with water beside it, and the lens goes into a drawer at the end. With a 5 cm lens in strong sun, black paper smokes in a few seconds and white paper takes much longer or does not smoke within 60 seconds, so the 60-second limit keeps the test short. Reading glasses are offered as a slower alternative. Sunglasses are worn only against the glare of the dot, and every step repeats that nobody looks at the Sun. The ice test uses ice from the same tray on identical steel plates, and checks every 5 minutes. The Mirror Sun needs a shaded wall at least 3 metres away. The steps say the spot is square close up and round far away, and that sunspots are too small to see. The Sun Print uses kite or tissue paper because it fades within a few days, and says to leave it longer if needed. Both games work for one child alone. how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people pictured the Sun as a giant fire. In the 1800s, scientists checked this idea with numbers. A ball of coal as big as the Sun, burning as brightly, would burn out in a few thousand years. But rocks and fossils showed that the Earth was far older. In 1854 Hermann von Helmholtz, a German scientist, suggested that the Sun shines because it is slowly shrinking, and the squeezing heats it. In 1862 Lord Kelvin, a famous British scientist, used this idea. He wrote that the Sun had probably not shone for 100 million years. Geologists, who study rocks, said the Earth's rocks needed much longer than that. In 1920 Arthur Eddington, an English astronomer, pointed to a new measurement by Francis Aston: a helium atom weighs a little less than four hydrogen atoms. If the Sun joins hydrogen into helium, the missing material could become energy, enough for billions of years. In 1925 Cecilia Payne showed that the Sun is mostly hydrogen, so the fuel is there. In 1939 Hans Bethe worked out how the joining happens. The Sun is not a fire, and it has shone for about 4.6 billion years.
how_we_found_out.who: Hermann von Helmholtz and Lord Kelvin, who were wrong, then Arthur Eddington, Francis Aston, Cecilia Payne and Hans Bethe
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the Sun was a giant fire, and later that it shone by slowly shrinking. Both would have used up the Sun in far less time than the Earth's rocks show it has existed. Fusion, joining hydrogen into helium, gives enough energy for billions of years.
